{{Short description|Category equipped with involution}}
In [[category theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a '''dagger category''' (also called '''involutive category''' or '''category with involution'''<ref name="Burgin" /><ref name="Lambek" />) is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] equipped with a certain structure called ''dagger'' or ''involution''.  The name dagger category was coined by Peter Selinger.<ref name="Selinger" />

== Formal definition ==

A '''dagger category''' is a category <math>\mathcal{C}</math> equipped with an [[Involution (mathematics)|involutive]] [[Contravariant functor|contravariant]] [[endofunctor]] <math>\dagger</math> which is the identity on [[Object (category theory)|objects]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dagger+category#with_a_contravariant_endofunctor | title=Dagger category in nLab }}</ref>

In detail, this means that:
* for all [[morphism]]s <math>f: A \to B</math>, there exists its [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] <math>f^\dagger: B \to A</math>
* for all morphisms <math>f</math>, <math>(f^\dagger)^\dagger = f</math>
* for all objects <math>A</math>, <math>\mathrm{id}_A^\dagger = \mathrm{id}_A</math>
* for all <math>f: A \to B</math> and <math>g: B \to C</math>, <math>(g \circ f)^\dagger = f^\dagger \circ g^\dagger: C \to A</math>

Note that in the previous definition, the term "adjoint" is used in a way analogous to (and inspired by) the [[linear algebra|linear-algebraic]] sense, not in [[Adjoint functors|the category-theoretic sense]].

Some sources<ref name="Springer" /> define a '''category with involution''' to be a dagger category with the additional property that its [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of morphisms is [[Partial order|partially ordered]] and that the order of morphisms is compatible with the composition of morphisms, that is <math>a < b</math> implies <math>a\circ c<b\circ c</math> for morphisms <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math> whenever their sources and targets are compatible.

== Examples ==

* The category '''Rel''' of [[Category of relations|sets and relations]] possesses a dagger structure: for a given [[Relation (mathematics)|relation]] <math>R:X \rightarrow Y</math> in '''Rel''', the relation <math>R^\dagger:Y \rightarrow X</math> is the [[converse relation|relational converse]] of <math> R</math>. In this example, a self-adjoint morphism is a [[symmetric relation]].
* The category '''Cob''' of [[Cobordism#Categorical aspects|cobordisms]] is a [[dagger compact category]], in particular it possesses a dagger structure.
* The category '''Hilb''' of [[Hilbert space]]s also possesses a dagger structure: Given a [[Hilbert space#Operators on Hilbert spaces|bounded linear map]] <math>f:A \rightarrow B</math>, the map <math>f^\dagger:B \rightarrow A</math> is just its [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] in the usual sense.
* Any [[monoid with involution]] is a dagger category with only one object. In fact, every [[endomorphism]] [[hom-set]] in a dagger category is not simply a [[monoid]], but a monoid with involution, because of the dagger.
* A [[discrete category]] is trivially a dagger category.
* A [[groupoid]] (and as trivial corollary, a [[Group (mathematics)|group]]) also has a dagger structure with the adjoint of a morphism being its inverse. In this case, all morphisms are unitary (definition below).

== Remarkable morphisms ==

In a dagger category <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, a morphism <math>f</math> is called
* '''unitary''' if <math>f^\dagger = f^{-1},</math>
* '''self-adjoint''' if <math>f^\dagger = f.</math> 
The latter is only possible for an [[endomorphism]] <math>f\colon A \to A</math>. The terms ''unitary'' and ''self-adjoint'' in the previous definition are taken from the category of Hilbert spaces, where the morphisms satisfying those properties are then [[Unitary transformation|unitary]] and [[self-adjoint]] in the usual sense.
